body.heading: The currency is kept promises
paragraphs: Every “I’ll send it tonight” that becomes an actual email is a coin in the bank. Every casual promise that evaporates is a small withdrawal — and people keep ledgers even when they never mention them. The balance is what they consult when you ask for something big.
This is good news: you do not need a dramatic occasion to become trustworthy. You need a hundred boring ones, handled straight.

body.heading: Be predictable in the small geography
paragraphs: Trust grows where people can predict you: you arrive when you said, you answer in the time you promised, you treat the waiter as you treat the director. Inconsistency in small courtesies reads as weather; people build their plans around climates, not storms they must guess at.
None of this requires perfection. It requires repair — the missed promise acknowledged before it is discovered, with a new one you can actually keep.

body.heading: Spend trust slowly, on purpose
paragraphs: When you have built trust, spend it carefully: ask for the significant favour plainly, explain why, and honour the answer. Trust spent transparently tends to return with interest; trust spent presumptuously — assuming the yes, skipping the thanks — devalues the whole account.
Relationships are long economies. Play the long game with small coins and you will find the vault surprisingly full when life makes a large withdrawal necessary.

takeaway: Keep the small promises, be predictable in courtesies, and spend trust transparently.
